frictionVectors.title: European energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong bargaining power as a major gas supplier to Europe, but pipeline and LNG relationships expose it to external pricing pressure and shifting European diversification strategies.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara and Sahel tensions
frictionVectors.details: Competition with Morocco and instability across the Sahel complicate Algeria's regional diplomacy, border security, and infrastructure ambitions.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of strategic logistics
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor is attracting major Western and Gulf financing because of its route to copper and cobalt, but Angola must prevent external operators from capturing disproportionate value from its transport infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependency
frictionVectors.details: Oil remains central to state revenue while declining production, foreign operators, and debt-service obligations constrain Luanda's ability to direct the full value of its resource base.

frictionVectors.title: Northern insecurity spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity moving south from the Sahel threatens parks, roads, and northern communities, increasing reliance on external security assistance and regional intelligence networks.

frictionVectors.title: Port and trade dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cotonou's importance gives Benin leverage, but reliance on foreign logistics capital and trade conditions with Nigeria leaves core commercial infrastructure vulnerable to external decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond market concentration
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has improved its negotiating position with major diamond partners, yet state revenues and export earnings remain exposed to global demand, synthetic stones, and external marketing networks.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign interest in copper, nickel, and other minerals offers diversification but could reproduce enclave extraction unless local processing and infrastructure linkages are secured.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security partnership
frictionVectors.details: Ouagadougou's reliance on Russian-linked security support reduces Western leverage but risks opaque concessions, political dependency, and weak accountability over strategic mining assets.

frictionVectors.title: Gold sector and insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Gold remains the principal source of foreign exchange, while insurgent violence, informal mining, and contested transport routes limit the state's ability to capture and secure production.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque Mineral Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Gold, nickel, and rare-mineral projects remain constrained by weak oversight and limited state bargaining power. Foreign operators and politically connected intermediaries capture substantial value relative to public revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-DRC Security Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Tensions involving Rwanda, eastern DRC armed groups, and cross-border movements complicate Burundi's security posture and divert resources from infrastructure and development.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Ports, digital connectivity, and renewable-energy projects rely heavily on foreign finance and concessionary partners, creating long-term leverage despite generally transparent governance.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Security Burden
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde's strategic Atlantic location exposes it to illicit trafficking and illegal fishing, while limited naval capacity makes outside security cooperation essential.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Strategic Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, ports, and energy projects expand connectivity but increase debt, procurement, and operational dependence. Oil, gas, timber, and mining contracts remain difficult for the state to monitor fully.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone and Far North Conflicts
frictionVectors.details: Insurgencies in the Northwest and Southwest, alongside Boko Haram-linked violence in the Far North, weaken territorial control and disrupt transport, agriculture, and extractive activity.

frictionVectors.title: Security-for-Resources Model
frictionVectors.details: Russian security personnel and aligned commercial networks retain major influence around regime protection and mining activity. This improves short-term battlefield resilience while limiting transparent state control of resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor and Border Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Poor roads and armed-group activity constrain access to gold, diamonds, and agricultural zones. Dependence on neighboring transit routes leaves Bangui vulnerable to external political and commercial pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Revenue Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Public finances remain heavily exposed to oil production and export infrastructure, leaving the government vulnerable to foreign operators, price swings, and disputes over revenue allocation.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan and Sahel Spillover
frictionVectors.details: The Sudan war and wider Sahel instability drive refugee flows, arms trafficking, and border militarization. External security partnerships remain important, limiting Chad's room for fully autonomous strategic choices.

highlights: Maritime connectivity depends on external partners

frictionVectors.title: France–Mayotte Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Moroni continues to contest French control of Mayotte, while migration management and French development assistance keep the issue politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Limited domestic infrastructure leaves Comoros reliant on foreign financing, shipping links, and external support to develop fisheries and maritime resources.

highlights: Critical minerals attract competing external powers

frictionVectors.title: M23–Rwanda Conflict
frictionVectors.details: M23 territorial gains and alleged Rwandan support continue to weaken Kinshasa's control in the east, while regional diplomacy struggles to produce a durable settlement.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Supply-Chain Competition
frictionVectors.details: Cobalt, copper, and coltan draw intense Chinese, Western, and regional interest, but weak oversight and insecurity limit the state's ability to capture full value.

highlights: Oil remains the fiscal and strategic core

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: State revenues and foreign-exchange earnings remain highly exposed to oil prices, constraining diversification and bargaining power over offshore assets.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction around ports, roads, and public facilities expand connectivity but can reduce fiscal flexibility and increase dependence on external creditors.

highlights: Abidjan is consolidating regional economic influence
Cocoa and energy value chains are expanding

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa Value-Capture Gap
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is increasing local processing, but farmers and the state remain exposed to volatile prices, foreign buyers, and limited control over downstream margins.

frictionVectors.title: French and Regional Security Footprint
frictionVectors.details: France remains an important economic and security partner, while instability in the Sahel raises pressure on Abidjan to balance external support with strategic autonomy.

highlights: Ports remain central to Ethiopia's trade access

frictionVectors.title: Great-Power Base Competition
frictionVectors.details: The concentration of American, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities gives Djibouti leverage but also subjects its sovereignty and policy choices to sustained external pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Port Debt and Ethiopia Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti's port economy is tied closely to Ethiopian trade and foreign-financed infrastructure, creating exposure to Addis Ababa's political shifts and creditor-related constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and strategic-asset financing
frictionVectors.details: Heavy external financing needs increase leverage for Gulf investors and multilateral lenders over major ports, land, and infrastructure. Cairo retains formal control but faces constrained policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea and Nile security
frictionVectors.details: Suez disruptions and regional instability threaten foreign-exchange earnings, while the Nile dispute with Ethiopia remains a core sovereignty concern.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependency
frictionVectors.details: Declining mature oil fields and volatile production leave the state exposed to foreign operators, price cycles, and reduced bargaining power over offshore assets.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure influence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign contractors remain important to public construction and energy projects, creating financing and maintenance dependencies despite strong state control.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Competition among regional and global powers around ports and shipping lanes increases pressure on Eritrea to provide access while it seeks to preserve strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign mining companies provide crucial capital and technical capacity, limiting domestic control over mineral development while sanctions and diplomatic isolation narrow alternatives.

frictionVectors.title: South African dependence
frictionVectors.details: Trade, transport corridors, electricity, and customs revenues remain closely tied to South Africa, limiting Eswatini's room for independent infrastructure and resource policy.

frictionVectors.title: Political legitimacy and investment
frictionVectors.details: Governance concerns complicate access to diversified external finance and can make strategic projects dependent on politically accommodating partners.

frictionVectors.title: Nile and regional power contest
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam expands Addis Ababa's control over electricity generation but continues to fuel tensions with Egypt and Sudan over Nile management.

frictionVectors.title: External finance and conflict recovery
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring, aid, and infrastructure financing give international lenders and partners significant influence as Ethiopia manages conflict-related reconstruction and foreign-exchange shortages.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and oil contract dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gabon is seeking greater state participation and local processing, but foreign operators and external capital remain central to oil, manganese, and infrastructure development.

frictionVectors.title: Military-led political transition
frictionVectors.details: The post-2023 transition has restored political order but leaves uncertainty over institutional checks, succession, and the durability of resource-governance reforms.

frictionVectors.title: Dependence on Senegalese trade access
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for transport connectivity, food flows, and regional market access, limiting its bargaining autonomy over infrastructure and customs arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and coastal resource pressure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing activity and weak enforcement continue to constrain local control of marine resources, while coastal erosion threatens ports, tourism, and settlements.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and environmental damage
frictionVectors.details: Unregulated gold mining is degrading water systems and farmland while exposing gaps in state enforcement and enabling illicit foreign-linked trading networks.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and critical-mineral competition
frictionVectors.details: Fiscal restructuring and IMF oversight constrain policy space, while competition for lithium, bauxite, and other minerals tests Ghana's ability to secure domestic value addition.

highlights: Junta balances China and the West

frictionVectors.title: Simandou infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore project could transform state revenues, but rail, port, and financing arrangements give major foreign consortiums substantial influence over Guinea's export architecture.

frictionVectors.title: Military rule and contract uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: The junta uses resource nationalism to strengthen legitimacy, yet delayed elections and opaque renegotiations raise concerns about governance, investor leverage, and elite capture.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew export dependency
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains heavily dependent on raw cashew exports, leaving farmers and public finances exposed to foreign buyers, price swings, and limited domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Political instability and illicit networks
frictionVectors.details: Recurring institutional tensions weaken oversight of ports and borders, creating openings for narcotics trafficking and politically connected external actors to influence state assets.

highlights: Ports and Corridors as Strategic Assets

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked fiscal reforms and external creditors constrain policy space. Chinese-financed rail and Gulf-linked port and logistics interests remain important to Kenya's infrastructure strategy.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu Corridor Contestation
frictionVectors.details: The Lamu Port-South Sudan-Ethiopia Transport Corridor offers strategic autonomy but faces insecurity, financing gaps, and competing regional trade interests.

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports to South Africa provide vital revenue but deepen dependence on South African financing, infrastructure, and downstream demand.

frictionVectors.title: Textiles and Mineral Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains vulnerable to external trade preferences and foreign-owned mining operations, leaving limited domestic control over value chains and employment.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign-controlled iron ore operations generate export earnings but limit Liberia's control over pricing, processing, and the distribution of resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Buchanan Logistics Corridor
frictionVectors.details: Rail and port infrastructure tied to mining concessions gives external operators significant influence over national transport assets and future mineral expansion.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Oil Gatekeepers
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and security networks continue to contest oil fields, terminals, and budget access, weakening the National Oil Corporation's effective national authority.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Patronage
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia, Egypt, the UAE, and European actors retain leverage through military, political, and migration-related arrangements, constraining Libya's strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Mineral Projects
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and graphite projects remain dominated by foreign capital, exposing Madagascar to commodity volatility while limiting domestic processing and fiscal capture.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Transport Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable power and weak roads increase reliance on external operators and project-specific infrastructure, reducing state control over strategic mineral corridors.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and reliance on IMF and donor support limit Malawi's autonomy over fiscal and development priorities. Foreign-exchange shortages continue to restrict fuel, fertilizer, and industrial imports.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Minerals Bottleneck
frictionVectors.details: Prospective uranium and rare-earth projects could diversify the economy, but weak transport, power, and processing capacity leave the country dependent on outside capital and export infrastructure.

highlights: Gold Sector Faces Security and Partner Risks

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The government has reduced Western engagement while deepening security cooperation with Russia-linked forces, creating new dependence without resolving insurgent threats.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Sovereignty Struggle
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is seeking greater state control and revenue from industrial gold operations, but disputes with international miners and insecurity around production zones threaten output and investment.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Gas Governance
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project offers major export and domestic-energy opportunities, but cross-border coordination with Senegal and reliance on foreign operators limit near-term national control.

frictionVectors.title: Export Corridor Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore revenues remain vulnerable to global prices and dependence on the state rail and port system, while Chinese and other external buyers retain substantial market influence.

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean Strategic Competition
frictionVectors.details: The Chagos sovereignty issue and the Diego Garcia military presence continue to constrain Mauritius's strategic autonomy despite diplomatic progress toward a settlement framework.

frictionVectors.title: External Trade and Finance Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius retains strong institutions and diversified services, but its shipping, tourism, and financial sectors remain sensitive to external demand, regulatory pressure, and major-power competition.

highlights: Phosphate and Green Industry Expand Leverage

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is using phosphate, fisheries, ports, and renewable-energy investment to consolidate control and attract partners in Western Sahara, sustaining opposition from the Polisario Front and Algeria.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Water Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Renewables, desalination, and green-hydrogen projects improve long-term resilience, but Morocco remains exposed to imported energy, external technology, and water stress.

highlights: Cabo Delgado insurgency strains state reach

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Security Corridor
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent attacks continue to threaten gas infrastructure and transport routes, leaving Mozambique reliant on foreign security support and private operators. Local grievances over land, jobs, and revenue-sharing remain unresolved.

frictionVectors.title: LNG Contract and Revenue Leverage
frictionVectors.details: International energy companies retain substantial influence over project financing, technology, and offtake. Maputo is seeking greater fiscal and domestic-development benefits while avoiding delays that could undermine the recovery.

highlights: Oil discoveries reshape national bargaining power
Green hydrogen race tests regulatory capacity

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Ownership
frictionVectors.details: Large offshore discoveries could strengthen state finances, but foreign operators control capital, deepwater technology, and project timelines. Namibia is pressing for stronger local-content and fiscal terms without deterring investment.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: European and Gulf-backed projects offer capital and export access but may lock Namibia into externally defined supply chains. Water use, land rights, transmission capacity, and domestic value addition are increasingly sensitive issues.

highlights: Junta nationalizes bargaining over uranium and oil
Sanctions and border closures raise infrastructure risk

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Extractives Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The authorities are seeking greater state control and revised terms from Western mining interests while courting Russian, Turkish, and other partners. The shift increases sovereignty claims but also raises operational and investment uncertainty.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Export Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Niger's crude exports depend on cross-border pipeline and terminal access, leaving the sector vulnerable to diplomatic disputes and regional insecurity. Political isolation also complicates maintenance, financing, and market access.

highlights: Refinery expansion boosts domestic energy leverage
Oil theft and grid weakness erode gains

frictionVectors.title: Refinery and Fuel-Market Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: The Dangote refinery and renewed investment in domestic processing could reduce dependence on imported fuel and improve bargaining power. Feedstock supply, regulation, and foreign-exchange constraints still limit strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Security and Oil Theft
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, sabotage, and weak infrastructure continue to reduce state capture of petroleum value. International operators retain influence over production and technology, while communities in the Niger Delta demand a larger share of benefits.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals and DRC Supply Chains
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda is positioning itself as a formal minerals-processing and trading hub, but allegations that conflict-linked minerals transit through the country expose it to sanctions and reputational pressure. External partners increasingly demand traceability and transparent certification.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Security Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Foreign aid, security cooperation, and investment remain important to Rwanda's development model. Its regional military posture and ties to actors in eastern DRC risk converting economic partnerships into diplomatic and commercial liabilities.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Licensing and Revenue Uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé and Príncipe continues to court foreign partners for potentially lucrative offshore blocks, but limited state capacity and uncertain commercial prospects constrain its bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The archipelago relies heavily on external financing and partners for ports, energy, and connectivity, creating influence competition without a single dominant external patron.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Operated Oil and Gas Projects
frictionVectors.details: Production from Sangomar and the Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project strengthens state revenues, but foreign operators, financing terms, and offshore technical dependence limit immediate national control.

frictionVectors.title: Fishing Access and Coastal Resources
frictionVectors.details: Industrial and foreign fishing access remains politically sensitive as coastal communities face pressure on fish stocks, enforcement capacity, and food security.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Infrastructure Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles leverages partnerships with India, China, Europe, and other maritime actors for surveillance and port capabilities while seeking to avoid strategic overdependence.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and Fisheries Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains vulnerable to external shocks and foreign control of tourism value chains, while sustainable management of fisheries and marine territory is difficult for a small state.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore and Mineral Contract Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mining and associated logistics remain central to growth, but foreign capital, export infrastructure, and contract negotiations limit domestic capture of mineral value.

frictionVectors.title: Freetown Port and Transport Finance
frictionVectors.details: Port expansion and transport projects bring needed connectivity but deepen reliance on external lenders and operators, raising concerns over debt exposure and strategic control.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Licensing and Federal Disputes
frictionVectors.details: Prospective offshore petroleum development is constrained by disputes among the federal government, member states, and foreign partners over licensing authority, revenue sharing, and security.

frictionVectors.title: Competing External Security and Port Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Turkish, Gulf, Western, and regional actors provide security and infrastructure support, but competing port relationships and foreign military access can dilute Mogadishu's strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Grid and port bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability and capacity constraints at Transnet rail and ports continue to weaken South Africa's control over mineral-export value chains. Private investment and foreign technology are increasingly important to restoring infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: The United States, China, and European partners are competing for influence over platinum-group metals, manganese, and other critical minerals. Pretoria is seeking diversified partnerships while resisting alignment that would narrow its diplomatic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-export corridor exposure
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's oil revenues depend on pipelines and export infrastructure traversing conflict-affected Sudan, leaving national finances exposed to external disruption and bargaining pressure. Production and fiscal control remain vulnerable to aging infrastructure and opaque contracting.

frictionVectors.title: Regional security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Political stabilization and protection of key transport routes rely heavily on neighboring states and international peace-support mechanisms. Localized fighting and delayed power-sharing continue to obstruct sovereign management of land and resource assets.

highlights: Red Sea access gains strategic value

frictionVectors.title: Competing control of gold networks
frictionVectors.details: Armed factions and external patrons compete over gold-producing areas and trading routes, diverting revenue away from national institutions. Cross-border smuggling and informal finance further weaken sovereign oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor militarization
frictionVectors.details: The Red Sea coast, Port Sudan, and inland corridors have become critical strategic infrastructure amid the conflict. Regional and Gulf actors are seeking access and influence, raising the risk that transport and maritime assets serve competing wartime interests.

frictionVectors.title: Dar es Salaam corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Expanded investment in ports, rail, and regional corridors is strengthening Tanzania's logistical leverage, but also increasing exposure to foreign lenders, operators, and strategic bargaining. Competition among Gulf, Chinese, Western, and regional partners is intensifying.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals governance
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is tightening local-processing and licensing expectations for graphite, nickel, and other minerals. The challenge is enforcing national value-add requirements without deterring capital or allowing opaque political intermediaries to capture rents.

frictionVectors.title: Port dependence and external finance
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé remains a major commercial and transshipment hub, but its expansion depends on foreign capital, shipping networks, and imported fuel and equipment. This creates leverage for outside actors over a strategically important national asset.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and insecurity near the northern frontier are increasing demands on Togo's security apparatus and transport corridors. External security cooperation is expanding, while instability in neighboring Burkina Faso risks disrupting trade and state reach.

highlights: EU migration leverage deepens external pressure

frictionVectors.title: ENERGY AND GAS DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains exposed to imported hydrocarbons and electricity-linked supply risks, particularly through its dependence on regional energy networks and external financing.

frictionVectors.title: EU MIGRATION BARGAIN
frictionVectors.details: European funding and cooperation are tied increasingly to migration control, creating sovereignty concerns and political friction over Tunisia’s role as a transit and containment partner.

highlights: Oil corridor advances under foreign capital

frictionVectors.title: EACOP FINANCING AND CLIMATE PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil project remains strategically important but faces international climate opposition, financing constraints, and scrutiny over land acquisition and environmental impacts.

frictionVectors.title: LAKE ALBERT RESOURCE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Uganda’s oil development relies heavily on foreign operators, Chinese participation, and Tanzanian export infrastructure, limiting near-term domestic control over the value chain.

highlights: Copper strategy shifts toward value addition
Debt restructuring restores limited room to maneuver

frictionVectors.title: COPPER OWNERSHIP AND BENEFICIATION
frictionVectors.details: Lusaka is seeking greater local processing and fiscal returns from copper, but foreign mining capital, concession terms, and global demand still strongly shape national resource outcomes.

frictionVectors.title: POWER SHORTFALL
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower vulnerability and drought-related generation losses threaten mining output and increase reliance on regional electricity imports and emergency infrastructure investment.

highlights: Critical minerals attract competing external interests

frictionVectors.title: LITHIUM AND MINERAL CONCESSIONS
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms remain central to lithium and other mineral development, while Zimbabwe’s push for domestic processing is constrained by capital shortages, technology gaps, and opaque licensing practices.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD FLOWS AND SANCTIONS EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: Informal gold trading, alleged smuggling, and sanctions-related financial constraints reduce state capture of mineral revenues and increase dependence on politically connected intermediaries.
